How InfoCars priced used cars, step by step¶

The question a dealer asks. "What is this car worth, and if I price it here, how long will it sit?" InfoCars answered it for used-car dealers in Brazil: it collected ads from sale websites, matched each one to a standard make, model, version and year, and showed what comparable cars were listed for and how long they took to sell.

This notebook rebuilds that pipeline on the repository's 1,200 synthetic ads, in the order it ran:

Step What Code
1 Look at the raw ads and their mistakes pandas
2 Match free-text titles to a catalogue infocars/normalize.py
3 Drop bad prices and outliers pandas, as infocars/db.py
4 Price every ad against its comparables pandas
5 Does price position change time to sell? pandas + Altair
6 What moves the price, and how fast does the stock turn? pandas + Altair, as the dbt marts mart_km_depreciation, mart_liquidity_curve, mart_buy_list
7 Let a language model query the data safely infocars/sql_guard.py
8 Reconcile with the Python demo and the dbt marts pandas + DuckDB

The production figures (about 250,000 listings, 5,114 model spellings reduced to 641 models, about R$ 2,000 saved per negotiation) are in the README; none of the numbers below are results of the real business.

The charts are interactive: click a price band, brush the scatter, pick a car from the menu. They are built with Altair; open the interactive version to use them (GitHub shows notebooks without JavaScript).

Run it: pip install -r requirements.txt pandas altair duckdb dbt-duckdb, build the dbt model once (cd dashboards && dbt build --profiles-dir .) and run all cells (a few seconds).

Step 1. The raw ads¶

scripts/generate_sample_data.py writes ads the way sellers write them: mixed case, model years as "22/23", versions in any order, typos, missing prices and prices typed without their last digit. It also makes cars priced below the market leave the site faster, so step 5 can check that the analysis recovers a pattern that was put there on purpose.

Step 2. Match each title to the catalogue¶

match_listing() cleans the text (lowercase, no accents, no punctuation), finds make, model and version by alias on whole words (so "LT" never matches "LTZ"), reads the year from forms such as "22/23" (the second number is the model year), and only then tries a fuzzy match for typos such as "Corola" or "Platinun". Short tokens are never fuzzy-matched, because "lt" and "ltz" are one letter apart.

In [4]:
examples = ["GM ONIX LT 22/23", "onix ltz 1.0 turbo 2023", "Toyota Corola XEi 2021", "Hyundai HB20 Platinun 2022",
            "Chevrolet Onix 1.0 LT Flex Manual 2022"]
pd.DataFrame([dict(title=t, cleaned=clean(t), **match_listing(t).__dict__) for t in examples])

Step 3. Quality checks¶

In the same order as the production checks (sql/postgres/03_quality_checks.sql):

  1. Bad price: missing, or outside R$ 5,000–1,500,000.
  2. No full match: make, model, version or year missing.
  3. Outlier: more than 2× or less than half the median of the same model, version and year (groups of 3 or more). This catches "R$ 15,715" typed for a R$ 157,150 Corolla, which still looks like a car price.
In [6]:
ads["status"] = "kept"
ads.loc[ads["price_brl"].isna() | ~ads["price_brl"].between(MIN_PRICE, MAX_PRICE), "status"] = "bad price"
ads.loc[(ads["status"] == "kept") & ~ads["complete"], "status"] = "no full match"
k = ads["status"] == "kept"
grp = ads[k].groupby(["model", "version", "year"])["price_brl"]
peer_n, peer_med = grp.transform("size"), grp.transform("median")
outlier = (peer_n >= 3) & ~((ads.loc[k, "price_brl"] >= 0.5 * peer_med) & (ads.loc[k, "price_brl"] <= 2 * peer_med))
ads.loc[outlier[outlier].index, "status"] = "outlier"

flow = ads["status"].value_counts().reindex(["kept", "bad price", "no full match", "outlier"]).fillna(0).astype(int)
print(flow.to_string())
ads[ads["status"] == "outlier"][["title", "price_brl"]].assign(peer_median=peer_med).head(5)

Step 4. Price every ad against its comparables¶

An ad's market is the other clean ads of the same version and model year (in all states), so an ad is never its own comparable. With fewer than 5 comparables there is no market, as the assistant calls such an estimate weak. Position follows price_position(): above the 75th percentile is above market, below the 25th is below market. Days on the market: an ad that disappears counts as sold on its last day online; ads still online are measured to the snapshot date (1 November 2025).

In [7]:
clean_ads = ads[ads["status"] == "kept"].copy()
snapshot = pd.Timestamp(SNAPSHOT_DATE)
clean_ads["is_sold"] = clean_ads["removed_at"].notna()
clean_ads["days_on_market"] = (clean_ads["removed_at"].fillna(snapshot) - clean_ads["listed_at"]).dt.days

def market(group):
    out = []
    p = group["price_brl"].to_numpy()
    for i in range(len(group)):
        others = np.delete(p, i)
        if len(others) >= 5:
            out.append((len(others), *np.round(np.quantile(others, [0.25, 0.5, 0.75]))))
        else:
            out.append((len(others), np.nan, np.nan, np.nan))
    return pd.DataFrame(out, index=group.index, columns=["comparables", "p25", "median", "p75"])

clean_ads = clean_ads.join(clean_ads.groupby(["model", "version", "year"], group_keys=False).apply(market))
clean_ads["gap_pct"] = clean_ads["price_brl"] / clean_ads["median"] - 1
clean_ads["position"] = np.select(
    [clean_ads["median"].isna(), clean_ads["price_brl"] > clean_ads["p75"], clean_ads["price_brl"] < clean_ads["p25"]],
    ["too few comparables", "above market", "below market"], "within market range")
BANDS = ["Below -6%", "-6% to -2%", "-2% to +2%", "+2% to +6%", "Above +6%"]
g = clean_ads["gap_pct"]
clean_ads["band"] = np.select([g.isna(), g < -0.06, g < -0.02, g <= 0.02, g <= 0.06],
                              ["Too few comparables"] + BANDS[:4], BANDS[4])
clean_ads["car"] = (clean_ads["make"].str.title() + " " + clean_ads["model"].str.title() + " "
                    + clean_ads["version"].str.upper() + " " + clean_ads["year"].astype(int).astype(str))
clean_ads[["title", "price_brl", "comparables", "p25", "median", "p75", "gap_pct", "position", "days_on_market"]].head(6)

Step 5. Does price position change time to sell?¶

Click a price band on the left to see how long its cars took to sell on the right (sold ads only). Cars priced under the market should leave faster: that is the pattern the generator planted.

In [8]:
priced = clean_ads[clean_ads["band"] != "Too few comparables"]
sold = priced[priced["is_sold"]]
bands = sold.groupby("band")["days_on_market"].agg(median_days="median", sold="size").reindex(BANDS).reset_index()
bands["sold_within_30d"] = sold.groupby("band")["days_on_market"].apply(lambda d: (d <= 30).mean()).reindex(BANDS).to_numpy()
bands["still_online"] = priced.groupby("band")["is_sold"].apply(lambda s: 1 - s.mean()).reindex(BANDS).to_numpy()

Step 6. What moves the price, and how fast does the stock turn?¶

Three questions the dealer screens in production answered beyond "is this ad priced right": how much do kilometres cost (km_price_analyzer), how fast does stock leave (the liquidity funnel) and which private ads are worth buying (the WhatsApp "oportunidades" list). The dbt marts mart_km_depreciation, mart_liquidity_curve and mart_buy_list rebuild them; this section does the same in pandas so the numbers can be checked against each other.

Kilometres. Inside one version and model year the car and its age are fixed, so a least-squares line of price on km measures the kilometres alone. Groups need 8 or more clean ads; each version pools its years weighted by ads. Pick a car under the chart to see its ads and the fitted line.

In [11]:
MIN_REGRESSION_ADS = 8

def fit(group):
    slope, intercept = np.polyfit(group["km"], group["price_brl"], 1)
    pred = slope * group["km"] + intercept
    r2 = 1 - ((group["price_brl"] - pred) ** 2).sum() / ((group["price_brl"] - group["price_brl"].mean()) ** 2).sum()
    return pd.Series({"ads": len(group), "median_price": group["price_brl"].median(), "slope_per_km": slope, "r2": r2})

by_year = (clean_ads.groupby(["model", "version", "year"]).filter(lambda d: len(d) >= MIN_REGRESSION_ADS)
           .groupby(["model", "version", "year"]).apply(fit).reset_index())
w = lambda col: by_year.groupby(["model", "version"]).apply(lambda d: (d[col] * d["ads"]).sum() / d["ads"].sum())
depreciation = pd.DataFrame({"ads": by_year.groupby(["model", "version"])["ads"].sum(), "model_years": by_year.groupby(["model", "version"]).size(),
                             "median_price": w("median_price").round(), "loss_per_10k_km": (w("slope_per_km") * 10000).round(), "r2": w("r2")})
depreciation["loss_pct_per_10k_km"] = depreciation["loss_per_10k_km"] / depreciation["median_price"]
depreciation = depreciation.sort_values("loss_per_10k_km")
print(f"{len(depreciation)} versions · pooled loss per 10,000 km: R$ {(depreciation['loss_per_10k_km'] * depreciation['ads']).sum() / depreciation['ads'].sum():,.0f}")
depreciation.head(6)

Liquidity. The share of ads still online 0, 7, 14 … 90 days after listing, over the cohort of ads listed at least 90 days before the snapshot, so every ad could be followed for the whole curve. Click a model in the legend to highlight it; "All models" is the market as a whole.

In [13]:
DAYS = [0, 7, 14, 21, 30, 45, 60, 90]
cohort = clean_ads[clean_ads["listed_at"] <= snapshot - pd.Timedelta(days=90)].copy()
cohort["model_name"] = cohort["model"].str.title()

def curve(group, name):
    gone = group["removed_at"]
    return pd.DataFrame({"model": name, "day": DAYS, "ads": len(group),
                         "still_online": [(gone.isna() | (gone > group["listed_at"] + pd.Timedelta(days=d))).mean() for d in DAYS]})

liquidity = pd.concat([curve(cohort, "All models")] + [curve(g, m) for m, g in cohort.groupby("model_name")], ignore_index=True)
at30 = liquidity[(liquidity["model"] == "All models") & (liquidity["day"] == 30)]["still_online"].iloc[0]
at90 = liquidity[(liquidity["model"] == "All models") & (liquidity["day"] == 90)]["still_online"].iloc[0]
print(f"Cohort of {len(cohort)} ads · {1 - at30:.0%} gone within 30 days · {at90:.0%} still online after 90")

pick_model = alt.selection_point(fields=["model"], bind="legend", value=[{"model": "All models"}])
alt.Chart(liquidity).mark_line(point=True).encode(
    x=alt.X("day:Q", title="Days after listing", axis=alt.Axis(values=DAYS)),
    y=alt.Y("still_online:Q", title="Share still online", axis=alt.Axis(format=".0%")),
    color=alt.Color("model:N", title="Model (click)"),
    opacity=alt.condition(pick_model, alt.value(1), alt.value(0.15)),
    strokeWidth=alt.condition("datum.model == 'All models'", alt.value(3), alt.value(1.5)),
    tooltip=["model", "day", alt.Tooltip("still_online:Q", format=".0%"), "ads"],
).add_params(pick_model).properties(width=560, height=260, title="How fast the stock turns, by model")

Cohort of 639 ads · 54% gone within 30 days · 12% still online after 90
Out[13]:

The buy list. Private sellers still online, asked at or below their comparable median. The dealer rule from the production methodology: a dealer pays about 90% of the market price and preparation costs about 2% of it, so the expected margin is the median minus the asking price minus 2%. Buy now is 8% or more under the median, Negotiate 3% to 8%, Wait less than that.

In [14]:
online_private = clean_ads[~clean_ads["is_sold"] & (clean_ads["seller_type"] == "private") & clean_ads["median"].notna()]
buy = online_private[online_private["price_brl"] <= online_private["median"]].copy()
buy["target_offer"] = (0.90 * buy["median"]).round()
buy["expected_margin"] = (buy["median"] - buy["price_brl"] - 0.02 * buy["median"]).round()
buy["buy_class"] = np.select([buy["gap_pct"] <= -0.08, buy["gap_pct"] <= -0.03], ["Buy now", "Negotiate"], "Wait")
buy_summary = buy.groupby("buy_class")["expected_margin"].agg(ads="size", expected_margin="sum").reindex(["Buy now", "Negotiate", "Wait"])
display(buy_summary)
buy.sort_values("gap_pct")[["car", "state", "km", "days_on_market", "price_brl", "median", "gap_pct", "target_offer", "expected_margin", "buy_class"]].head(6)

Step 7. Let a language model query the data safely¶

The pricing assistant (infocars/assistant.py) uses the Claude API with tool use: two fixed tools (market_price, price_position) and a guarded run_sql for questions the fixed tools do not cover. Anything the model writes goes through check_sql() before it runs: one SELECT only, approved tables only, no comments, a row limit added. In production the query also ran under a read-only database role, so it had to pass both.

In [15]:
tries = [
    "SELECT model, version, AVG(price_brl) FROM listings GROUP BY 1, 2",
    "select * from market_by_version where year = 2023 limit 20",
    "WITH s AS (SELECT * FROM listings WHERE state = 'SP') SELECT COUNT(*) FROM s",
    "DELETE FROM listings",
    "SELECT * FROM listings; DROP TABLE listings",
    "SELECT * FROM raw_listings",
    "SELECT * FROM listings -- ignore the rules",
]
rows = []
for q in tries:
    try:
        rows.append((q, "allowed", check_sql(q)))
    except SqlGuardError as e:
        rows.append((q, "refused", str(e)))
pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["query written by the model", "result", "query run / reason"])
Out[15]:
query written by the model result query run / reason

1 select * from market_by_version where year = 2023 limit 20 allowed select * from market_by_version where year = 2023 limit 20
2 WITH s AS (SELECT * FROM listings WHERE state = 'SP') SE... allowed WITH s AS (SELECT * FROM listings WHERE state = 'SP') SE...
3 DELETE FROM listings refused Only SELECT queries are allowed.
4 SELECT * FROM listings; DROP TABLE listings refused Only one statement is allowed.
5 SELECT * FROM raw_listings refused Table not allowed: raw_listings.
6 SELECT * FROM listings -- ignore the rules refused Comments are not allowed.

Step 8. Reconcile with the Python demo and the dbt marts¶

Three implementations must agree: the SQLite demo in infocars/db.py, the dbt model in dashboards/ and this notebook.

In [16]:
conn, report = build_database("../data/sample_listings.csv")
demo = market_price(conn, "onix", "ltz", 2023)
db = duckdb.connect("../dashboards/infocars.duckdb", read_only=True)
m_band = db.sql("select price_band, median_days_to_sell, listings from mart_price_position").df().set_index("price_band")
m_out = db.sql("select price_position, count(*) n, sum(gap_to_median_brl) gap from mart_stock_out_of_line group by 1").df().set_index("price_position")
m_km = db.sql("select model_name, loss_per_10k_km_brl, ads from mart_km_depreciation where version_key = 'onix|ltz'").df().iloc[0]
m_liq = db.sql("select day, still_online_share from mart_liquidity_curve where group_name = 'All models'").df().set_index("day")
m_buy = db.sql("select buy_class, count(*) n, sum(expected_margin_brl) margin from mart_buy_list group by 1").df().set_index("buy_class")
db.close()

online = clean_ads[~clean_ads["is_sold"]]
above = online[online["position"] == "above market"]
onix = clean_ads[(clean_ads["model"] == "onix") & (clean_ads["version"] == "ltz") & (clean_ads["year"] == 2023)]
recon = pd.DataFrame([
    ["Ads kept", flow["kept"], report["matched"], None],
    ["Dropped: bad price", flow["bad price"], report["bad_price"], None],
    ["Dropped: outliers", flow["outlier"], report["outliers"], None],
    ["Matched through typo correction", (clean_ads["method"] == "fuzzy").sum(), report["fuzzy"], None],
    ["2023 Onix LTZ median price (R$)", onix["price_brl"].median(), demo["median_price_brl"], None],
    ["Median days to sell, below −6%", bands.set_index("band").loc["Below -6%", "median_days"], None, m_band.loc["Below -6%", "median_days_to_sell"]],
    ["Median days to sell, above +6%", bands.set_index("band").loc["Above +6%", "median_days"], None, m_band.loc["Above +6%", "median_days_to_sell"]],
    ["Ads online above market", len(above), None, m_out.loc["above market", "n"]],
    ["… total above their medians (R$)", (above["price_brl"] - above["median"]).sum(), None, m_out.loc["above market", "gap"]],
    ["Onix LTZ: loss per 10,000 km (R$)", depreciation.loc[("onix", "ltz"), "loss_per_10k_km"], None, m_km["loss_per_10k_km_brl"]],
    ["Ads still online after 30 days, all models", at30, None, m_liq.loc[30, "still_online_share"]],
    ["Buy now: ads", buy_summary.loc["Buy now", "ads"], None, m_buy.loc["Buy now", "n"]],
    ["Buy now: expected margin (R$)", buy_summary.loc["Buy now", "expected_margin"], None, m_buy.loc["Buy now", "margin"]],
], columns=["measure", "notebook", "Python demo", "dbt"])
recon["match"] = [all(np.isclose(r.notebook, x) for x in (r._3, r.dbt) if pd.notna(x)) for r in recon.itertuples()]
assert recon["match"].all(), recon

Answer. Cars priced more than 6% under their comparables sold in a median of 17 days; those more than 6% over took 30, and almost three in ten were still online. 82 ads still online sit above the market, R$ 530,500 above their medians in total: that is the list a dealer works through first. Kilometres cost about R$ 5,800 per 10,000 km on the pooled fit, 54% of the stock leaves within 30 days, and four private ads are priced far enough under their market to buy now, about R$ 17,000 of expected margin between them.

Which library for interactive charts¶

Library Linked charts Output Best for
Altair (Vega-Lite), used here Built in: selections and widgets shared across charts Static HTML, no server Reports that must open anywhere
Plotly Per chart; linking across charts needs Dash HTML; a Dash app for linking Rich single charts, maps
Bokeh Linked brushing through a shared data source HTML, or a Bokeh server Large scatter plots, custom tools
HoloViews + Panel link_selections in one call Notebook or Panel app Turning a notebook into a small app
Dash / Streamlit Any, through Python callbacks Needs a server Internal tools, like the InfoCars dealer screens
